_about: One or two sentences of context per cuisine, shown in the side panel under the numbers. Keys are DOHMH cuisine labels. Keep them factual; build.py fills in the numbers.
American: The default label: 1 in 6 restaurants. Its peak is a data quirk: every concession stand at Yankee Stadium has its own permit.
Asian/Asian Fusion: This catch-all label holds much of the city's Himalayan food. The peak, where Elmhurst meets Woodside and Jackson Heights, is mostly Nepali and Tibetan momo shops.
Bagels/Pretzels: Bagel shops are everywhere, so no neighborhood stands out much.
Bakery Products/Desserts: The strongest pockets are Chinese bakeries along Avenue U in southern Brooklyn and in Sunset Park.
Caribbean: Flatbush and East Flatbush, officially named Little Caribbean in 2017, hold the biggest cluster. South Ozone Park and Richmond Hill in Queens, home to many Guyanese and Trinidadian New Yorkers, hold the second.
Chicken: Fried-chicken counters, chains included. Strongest in Crown Heights, Jamaica and the Bronx.
Chinese: Manhattan's Chinatown is the oldest, but Sunset Park's 8th Avenue and Flushing's Main Street now have a higher share of Chinese restaurants, many of them Fujianese and Sichuan.
Donuts: Mostly Dunkin'. The peak is a data quirk: Dunkin' stands on the Staten Island Ferry boats are registered at the Whitehall terminal.
Eastern European: Brighton Beach, nicknamed Little Odessa, has Russian, Ukrainian, Georgian and Central Asian restaurants, and one of the tightest clusters of any cuisine.
French: Fine dining and bistros on the Upper East Side and in the West Village.
Frozen Desserts: Ice cream, Italian ices and frozen yogurt. Strongest on Staten Island's East Shore and at Coney Island.
Fusion: A catch-all label with no real center.
Greek: Astoria is the city's Greek neighborhood, with tavernas and cafés around Ditmars Boulevard and 30th Avenue.
Hamburgers: Mostly McDonald's, Burger King and White Castle. The highest shares are in the South Bronx.
Indian: The strongest pocket isn't Jackson Heights but Richmond Hill and South Ozone Park, a center of Punjabi Sikh life in Queens.
Irish: Pubs in Woodside and Sunnyside, long-time Irish neighborhoods in Queens.
Italian: Little Italy is now a few blocks of Mulberry Street. Arthur Avenue in the Bronx's Belmont has a much higher share of Italian restaurants.
Japanese: One of the least clustered cuisines: sushi and ramen are spread across the city. Its highest share is in East Midtown.
Jewish/Kosher: Midwood, Homecrest and Borough Park are centers of Orthodox Jewish life, and South Williamsburg is Hasidic. Rego Park and Forest Hills have large Bukharian Jewish communities.
Juice, Smoothies, Fruit Salads: Juice bars and bubble tea. Strongest in Flatbush and Corona.
Korean: Koreatown on West 32nd Street has the most Korean restaurants, but they're a small share of a busy block. Along Northern Boulevard in Murray Hill and East Flushing, Queens, they're the majority.
Latin American: A broad label for South and Central American food. Corona and Jackson Heights have large Ecuadorian and Colombian communities, and Inwood is largely Dominican.
Mediterranean: A loose label. Strongest in Bay Ridge, where Arab-American shops and restaurants line 5th Avenue.
Mexican: Elmhurst, East Harlem, Mott Haven and Sunset Park are where many Mexican New Yorkers, a large share of them from Puebla, live.
Middle Eastern: Steinway Street in Astoria, known as Little Egypt, has the biggest cluster, with Bay Ridge close behind.
New American: Mostly sit-down restaurants in Brooklyn Heights, the Upper West Side and Williamsburg.
Peruvian: Pollo a la brasa and cevicherías in Elmhurst, Jackson Heights and Woodhaven.
Pizza: Pizza is everywhere. Its strongest pockets are all in the Bronx, not the Manhattan and Brooklyn spots famous for it.
Salads: Sweetgreen and Just Salad: chains that follow office workers to SoHo, the Upper East Side and the Financial District.
Sandwiches: Delis and sandwich chains, spread thin across the city.
Sandwiches/Salads/Mixed Buffet: Delis and buffets, spread thin across the city.
Seafood: Highest by the water at Coney Island, then scattered across the city.
Southeast Asian: Vietnamese, Malaysian and Indonesian restaurants, scattered across Elmhurst and southern Brooklyn.
Spanish: Despite the name, mostly Latin American spots: Dominican, Peruvian and empanada shops in Woodhaven, Washington Heights and the Bronx.
Steakhouse: Few and scattered. Midtown's famous steakhouses are a tiny share of the restaurants around them.
Tex-Mex: Chipotle and taco shops, spread thin across the city.
Thai: Elmhurst, home to much of the city's Thai community, has by far the highest share.
